proves: the five cross-axis alignments each place a child differently, and shows the two properties that change a child's own SIZE rather than its position
checkable: 392x136 on white, eight 88x56 cells at x=8, 104, 200 and 296, rows at y=8 and y=72. Every cell holds three children - red 24 wide, blue 30, green 20 - sized by a spacer inside them rather than by a height of their own, and spread with space-between. Read each child's bounding box relative to its cell. flex-start: red (0,0,24,20), blue (31,0,30,32), green (68,0,20,44). center: red (0,18), blue (31,12), green (68,6). flex-end: red (0,36), blue (31,24), green (68,12). stretch: all three 56 tall - red (0,0,24,56), blue (31,0,30,56), green (68,0,20,56). baseline on boxes: red (0,24), blue (31,12), green (68,0).
why_the_children_have_no_height: align-items: stretch changes the size of a child that has no cross size of its own, and nothing else. An item with its own height is stretched to exactly the height it already had - so a fixture built that way draws `stretch` as a copy of `flex-start` and reports a covered alignment that was never exercised. The spacer inside each child gives it an intrinsic height without giving it a height.
baseline_on_boxes_is_not_the_defect: a box's baseline IS its bottom margin edge, in Chrome as much as here, so this cell agrees with the browser and says nothing about the taffy baseline gap. That defect needs a MEASURED LEAF - text - and it is pinned in `baseline-alignment`. Thirty Chrome rows of this matrix also agree on baseline for the same reason, and a reader who took them as covering Align::Baseline would be wrong.
wrap_pins_a_defect: the wrap cells hold SIX children in six DISTINCT colours, in a box that fits three. wrap: red (0,0,24,44), blue (24,0,30,44), green (54,0,20,44) on the first line and amber, violet and teal at y=44, clipped to 12 rows by the cell's own bottom edge. wrap-reverse: the same two lines the other way up AND bottom-aligned - amber, violet and teal at y=-32, hanging off the top of the cell and over the row above it, and red, blue and green at y=12 so the last line's bottom sits on the cell's bottom edge. That is Chrome's placement to the pixel.
status: PINS NO DEFECT ANY MORE. It pinned one, in the wrap-reverse cell: the reversed line stack was packed from the top where Chrome bottom-aligns it, 32 pixels out. Fixed in layout.rs by bottom_align_reversed_wraps - taffy applies css-align-3's SAFE fallback when a distributed alignment overflows, which throws the reversal away at exactly the moment it would push content out of the box, and Chrome keeps it. Every other cell was correct behaviour already, confirmed against Chrome by the thirty-case matrix and the three wrapping cases in chrome_tables.rs.
why_six_colours: the first version of these two cells drew the same three children twice. Two lines of identical colours in identical columns are ONE picture: the wrap and wrap-reverse cells came out pixel-identical and a per-colour bounding box merged both lines into one tall box. It read as 'wrapping does nothing' and wrapping was working. A cell has to be able to tell its children apart before it can say where they went - the same rule as a mask image with no alpha, one level out.
the_reversed_line_leaves_the_cell: amber, violet and teal now draw ABOVE this cell, over the row of cells above it. That is not bleed to be clipped away: a flex line that overflows a box hangs out of it in a browser too, since nothing here sets overflow: hidden. A future version of this fixture that hid the overflow would stop being able to see the property at all.
